findings.quote: He was to evacuate the cities and territory specified.
findings.problem: The Greek reads ἐκχωρείτω δὲ πόλεων καὶ χώρας * **. - the text breaks off after χώρας (lacuna marked by asterisks); the list of cities and territory is lost. The English reads on as if the clause were whole and implies a specification that is not in the surviving text.
findings.proposed_fix: He was to withdraw from cities and territory [...]. [The text is broken off here; the list of places is lost.]

findings.quote: at the season when he also paid the Romans
findings.problem: Greek τῷ ἐπιβαλλομένῳ * καιρῷ, ᾧ καὶ τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἀποδίδωσι has a single-asterisk gap after ἐπιβαλλομένῳ that the English does not mark; the verb is also present tense (ἀποδίδωσι).
findings.proposed_fix: at the appropriate [...] time, at which he also pays the Romans

units.note: Also ambiguous, left unchanged: μὴ διιέναι ... διὰ τῆς αὑτῶν χώρας ἐπὶ Ῥωμαίους καὶ τοὺς συμμάχους πολεμίους. The Greek is awkward (ἐπὶ Ῥωμαίους is the target, πολεμίους has no clear role) and could mean either 'not to march against the Romans as enemies' or, as in Livy and the English, 'not to let enemies of Rome pass'. The English resolves it silently; no fix proposed. All numbers checked and correct: 12,000 talents, 12 years, 1,000 a year, 80 pounds, 540,000 modii, 350 talents over 5 years at 70 a year, 127 talents 1,208 drachmas, 20 hostages, every 3 years, ages 18 to 45, 10 decked ships, 30 oars. Names correct.

findings.problem: Greek Λεύκιον τὸν ἀδελφόν has no genitive; the subject of the sentence is ὁ στρατηγός, so Lucius is the commander's brother (Lucius Manlius, brother of Gnaeus Manlius Vulso), not a brother of Thermus. English 'his brother' reads as Thermus's brother, which is a wrong identity.

units.note: The participle κεκομικότα is singular, so 'who had only just brought back the money' strictly agrees with one man; the Greek order leaves it ambiguous which, and the existing English dash-clause preserves that.
300 talents, Manlius the proconsul, Ariarathes: all correct.
Greek is badly mutilated; the English marks the gap with [...] and says so, and adds no invented content.
